newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania nationalists protest against Ukraine pact.
newsitem.headline: Romania nationalists protest against Ukraine pact.

text.p: Around 1,000 Romanian nationalists protested in Bucharest on Thursday against a key treaty with ex-Soviet Ukraine, accusing the centrist government of selling off the Balkan country to the West.
"Down with the government of traitors, down with the Romanian-Hungarian government," the protesters jeered as they marched towards the government's offices in the city centre.

The protest was staged by the Greater Romania Party (PRM), which won a tiny five percent of the vote in last year's elections, when centrists pushed ex-communists out of office for the first time in seven years.

PRM leader Corneliu Vadim Tudor, whose newspapers often contain anti-Semitic and xenophobic attacks, accused reformist President Emil Constantinescu of rushing to sign the deal with Kiev to woo friends in the West.

Constantinescu will meet Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma in Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta on June 2, to sign the long-delayed pact -- seen by many in the West as boosting Romania's outsider bid for first-wave admission to NATO.
"Emil Constantinescu plans to go to Constanta to carry out the most shameful act of national treason," Tudor said, drawing boos against the government from his supporters.

Bucharest has dropped its previous insistence that Kiev should atone for the loss of former Romanian heartlands seized by the Kremlin under a 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact which carved up much of eastern Europe.

The nationalist protesters carried old maps of northern Bucovina, Herta and southern Bessarabia -- lost to Moscow and now part of modern-day Ukraine. They dispersed later on Thursday, when a spring storm swept the city.
Romania won praise from Western leaders for signing a pact with Hungary last year, settling old rifts over borders and minorities.

The new centrist leaders hope that a similar deal with Ukraine will boost Romania's chances of being invited to join, along with favourited Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, when the Alliance announces its first eastward expansion at a Madrid summit in July.
Constantinescu, 57, himself born in what is now ex-Soviet Moldova, defended the treaty with Kiev.
"Nobody can speak for all the Romanians, or in the name of those living in Ukraine or elsewhere," he said before leaving for a visit to Greece on Thursday.
